Case File — Product Build

Sparq: an operations platform built from discovery to shipped MVP

Debt-resolution teams ran lead distribution, outbound calling, compliance, and production tracking across disconnected tools. This is the record of building the system that replaced them.

Role Product Owner & Technical Architect
Stack Flutter · Firebase · Firestore
Status MVP live, in refinement

I owned this build end to end — from sitting with the business to understand how debt-resolution work actually happens, through mapping and planning it, to directing an AI-assisted build of the working system. Nobody handed me a spec. I wrote it, because I wrote the process map first.

§1

How it was built

01Discovery

Learning the process before touching a tool

Sat with the operation to understand how leads actually move — intake, distribution, outreach, compliance holds, collections, escalation to counsel. Mapped the full workflow in Miro before any technical decision got made, so the system would fit how the work really happens, not a guess at it.

02Feasibility

Proving the idea was buildable before committing to it

Tested whether a single codebase could unify what had been separate tools — a distribution system, a dialer, a production board, a compliance layer — without a dedicated backend team. Firestore's real-time listeners and a seeded 16-role demo dataset made it possible to validate every role's path through the app before a single real user touched it.

03Planning

Sequencing the build, architecting before coding

Scoped and sequenced delivery in Jira, and set the technical approach ahead of implementation: a 17-service architecture split cleanly between real-time, listener-backed services and static utilities, and a role-access matrix every later screen would have to respect. The pattern came first so the features had something to slot into.

04Build

AI-assisted implementation, directed line by line

Used Claude Code as the implementation layer — I made every architectural, compliance, and UX call; the AI executed against direction I reviewed and corrected in real time. This is what made ~97,000 lines of production Dart possible at solo-founder speed.

§2

What shipped

The MVP covers the full operational loop — a lead comes in, gets routed, gets worked, gets tracked, and rolls up into performance data, with compliance enforced at every step rather than bolted on after.

Lead Distribution
Round-robin routing, configurable distribution rules, channel and campaign management.
Compliance-Aware Dialer
Live call scripts, DNC/opt-out gating, consent logging, FDCPA call-frequency enforcement, an auto-progressing power dialer.
Debt Validation Workflow
In-call dispute handling that sets real case status and fires the required regulatory notice, not a cosmetic checkbox.
Live Production Board
Real-time team status, callback backlog, and case ledgers grouped by portfolio — the tool contractors actually work from all day.
Role-Gated Access
16 distinct roles, field-level gating on PII and financial data, route-level access enforced app-wide.
Performance & GTM
Goal tracking, appraisals, skill tiers, and a documentation site covering the whole system for handoff.
§3

Inside the system

All data shown is synthetic seed/demo data. Names, portfolio labels, and figures below are still blacked out on top of that, since a public case study shouldn't normalize showing anything shaped like real personal or financial data — even fake.

GreenScreen — live team production board, Call Backs view
Dialer — live call panel with Mini GreenScreen roster
Dashboard — role-scoped KPIs and annual revenue overview
Portfolio — role-gated lead management view
Where the plan changed

The original plan had one screen serving as the contractor's daily data-entry point. Usability testing said otherwise — it had been designed for executives and came out KPI-heavy, not usable for the people entering data all day. Rather than force the original plan, I scoped and shipped a second screen built around how contractors actually needed to work. That's the difference between running a plan and running a product.

§4

Where it stands now

The system is past first-build and into refinement — the harder, less visible work of making sure it measures the right thing. Recent iteration has gone into things that only surface once real usage patterns show up: rebuilding the round-robin queue to route by actual live availability instead of a fixed order, fixing a status field that three different screens each wrote independently without syncing, and correcting what "cases worked" and "pending callbacks" should really count once the definitions got tested against a full day of use.

§5

Projected impact

Sparq is at MVP stage — pre-live, no production usage to measure yet. What follows is what the architecture is built to change, reasoned from what the old process required versus what the system now enforces automatically, not a claimed result.

Tooling
leads, calls, compliance, and production tracked across separate spreadsheets and disconnected tools → one system, one source of truth per case
Compliance
DNC, consent, and call-frequency rules relied on agent training and manual policy adherence → enforced in the call flow itself — a blocked number can't be dialed, a limit can't be silently exceeded
Lead routing
assignment was manual or ad hoc, case by case → automatic round-robin and rule-based distribution the moment a lead lands
Visibility
production numbers assembled by hand at day's end → a live board showing callback backlog and case status a manager can act on same-day
Audit trail
compliance actions documented as a separate manual step, easy to skip under pressure → logged automatically as part of the workflow that triggered them
